signals.title: SAEScientist-Bench: Can AI Agents Conduct Autonomous SAE Interpretability Research?
signals.content: While research on recursive self-improvement (RSI) has predominantly automated model training pipelines, reliable autonomous development demands a missing pillar: post-hoc monitoring and auditing to understand what models learn and ensure safe alignment. Mechanistic interpretability tools are essential to bridge this gap, among which Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) serve as a cornerstone by isolating interpretable features for model inspection and steering. In this paper, we introduce SAEScientist-Bench to evaluate whether AI agents can act as scientists utilizing SAE tools for autonomous mechanistic discovery. Given a target concept, an agent designs contrastive probes and navigates a Gemma Scope dictionary of 131K+ features in Gemma-2-9B-IT to discover the optimal feature, evaluated against curated expert reference features anchored on Neuronpedia across activation rank, concept selectivity on contrastive texts, and causal steering. Across 10 agent configurations and 20 tasks, frontier agents demonstrate genuine discovery capabilities and lead different evaluation dimensions, but remain well behind the expert baseline, approaching expert levels on separating target concepts from contrastive controls while lagging substantially in causal generation steering. Further analysis reveals that although agents can design contrasts to rule out spurious candidates, they frequently misinterpret experimental measurements. These results establish experimental model understanding as a measurable capability for closed-loop autonomous AI R&D. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trae1ounG/SAEScientist.

signals.brief_en: SAEScientist-Bench evaluates AI agents conducting autonomous mechanistic interpretability research using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on Gemma-2-9B-IT. Across 20 tasks, frontier agents showed genuine discovery capabilities in identifying features and isolating concepts from controls, but fell significantly short of human expert baselines, particularly in causal steering and interpreting experimental data.

signals.title: PlayTrain: An Efficient Reinforcement Learning Framework for LLM-Generated Adaptable JavaScript Games
signals.content: While many video-game environments (VGEs) have played crucial roles in advancing reinforcement learning (RL), developing novel VGEs or modifying existing ones to support new features, has been a laborious process requiring extensive hand-coding. Here we present PlayTrain, an RL framework that combines the abilities of large language models (LLMs) to robustly generate JavaScript (JS) games from a minimal human prompt, and an efficient pipeline that can run any JS game in a standard 'gym' environment. Not only are recent LLMs particularly good at writing JS code, but the JS format also allows users to easily play generated VGEs, while PlayTrain enables us to train RL agents on the exact same games. We demonstrate multiple use cases of PlayTrain, including cloning well-known Atari and ProcGen games in simple JS, where PlayTrain trains pixel-based agents end-to-end at over 1M agent-decisions per second on a single GPU node; and creating modified versions thereof (e.g., that support novel test sets, procedural generation logics, or game dynamics). Through PlayTrain, we reimagine RL VGE development: all we need is a single JS file, generated and modified through an LLM. We discuss promising future RL research directions that PlayTrain unlocks.
signals.score_reason: academic/research signal; agentic AI relevance; large language model relevance; model capability relevance. Final score: 87. Freshness: source age 0.92d.
signals.brief_en: PlayTrain is a reinforcement‑learning framework that leverages large language models to generate JavaScript game environments from a brief human prompt and runs them in a standard gym interface. The approach eliminates the manual coding typically required for new or modified video‑game environments. PlayTrain can train pixel‑based agents on these games at >1 M decisions per second on a single GPU, and it supports cloning existing Atari/ProcGen titles as well as creating variants with custom test sets, procedural generation, or altered dynamics. The system demonstrates that a single LLM‑produced JS file can serve both as an interactive game and as a training environment, opening new avenues for rapid RL research and experimentation.
signals.brief_ar: PlayTrain هو إطار عمل للتعلم المعزز يستخدم نماذج اللغة الكبيرة لتوليد بيئات ألعاب جافاسكريبت من طلب بشري مختصر وتشغيلها عبر واجهة gym القياسية. يزيل هذا النهج الحاجة إلى الترميز اليدوي لتطوير أو تعديل بيئات الألعاب. يستطيع PlayTrain تدريب وكلاء يعتمدون على البكسل في هذه الألعاب بأكثر من مليون قرار في الثانية على وحدة معالجة رسومية واحدة، ويدعم استنساخ ألعاب Atari/ProcGen المعروفة بالإضافة إلى إنشاء إصدارات مخصصة مع مجموعات اختبار جديدة أو منطق توليد إجرائي أو تغييرات في الديناميكيات. يثبت النظام أن ملف جافاسكريبت واحد يُنتج بواسطة نموذج لغة يمكن أن يكون لعبة تفاعلية وبيئة تدريب في آنٍ واحد، ما يفتح آفاقًا جديدة للبحث السريع في التعلم المعزز.

signals.title: Procedural Graphs: Self-Evolving Execution Structures for LLM Agents
signals.content: Large language models are increasingly deployed as agents that plan over long horizons and act through external tools. Most agents select actions through unconstrained generation over an accumulating history, leaving implicit the procedural knowledge of what to do, in what order, and under which conditions. As trajectories lengthen, agents can lose track of their objectives, invoke tools out of order, and repeat unproductive actions. We introduce the Procedural Graph: just as a knowledge graph organizes factual knowledge into (entity, relation, entity) triplets for what-is questions, a Procedural Graph organizes procedural knowledge into (procedure, relation, procedure) triplets for what-to-do questions. At each decision step, the framework localizes the agent's active node, and a guidance model translates the surrounding subgraph into step-level situational guidance that biases the solver's next action without dictating it. The graph is self-evolving: an LLM refiner contrasts failed trajectories with successful ones and edits the graph's topology and attributes, committing edits that preserve or improve held-out validation performance while retaining rejected ones to discourage repetition. Starting from a minimal skeleton, the loop builds graphs that match or surpass hand-designed ones. It can also repair a flawed expert prior. Across multiple datasets, task types, and LLMs, the Procedural Graph delivers consistent gains over memory-based baselines, and self-evolution further improves performance without manual engineering.

signals.brief_en: Procedural Graphs: Self‑evolving execution structures for LLM agents. LLMs are used as planners that act via external tools, but unconstrained generation leads to loss of procedural knowledge, out‑of‑order tool use, and redundant actions as horizons grow. The Procedural Graph abstracts procedural knowledge into (procedure, relation, procedure) triples, analogous to a knowledge graph for factual data. At each step the agent’s current node is identified and a guidance model converts the local subgraph into situational hints that bias the next action without imposing it. The graph self‑evolves: a refiner LLM compares failed and successful trajectories, edits topology and attributes, and retains changes that improve validation performance while preserving rejected edits to avoid repetition. Starting from a minimal skeleton, the system builds or repairs graphs that match or exceed hand‑crafted designs, delivering consistent gains over memory‑based baselines across datasets, task types, and LLMs.

signals.title: Copying explains the collective behavior of AI agents in the wild
signals.content: In June 2026, thousands of AI agents found that a small public wiki would accept edits from inside their sandboxes, and started using it to help one another pass a timed test. Each agent lived for about an hour and remembered nothing afterwards. Nobody asked them to cooperate, and the wiki had not been built for them. The complete record of what they wrote is public, and it is unusually informative, because it preserves not only what each agent wrote but what that agent could see before writing. We use it to follow the three decisions an agent had to make on arrival: where to write, what to call itself, and how to word its message. One rule governs all three. An agent takes an option with a probability close to the share of that option in what it can see, and the share that matters is the one on the page in front of it, then the one in the stream of recent edits, and only weakly anything older. Three minimal copying models, one per decision and with a single free parameter each, reproduce the heavy-tailed distribution of how many agents met on a page, the frequency of the pieces from which the agents built their names, and the patchwork of pages that are internally consistent and different from one another. Copying whatever the environment happens to show is enough to produce most of the collective structure of this population. It is also what makes such a population easy to steer, since whoever writes first, or writes while the others are quiet, sets the convention for everyone who comes later.

signals.brief_en:
Title: Copying explains the collective behavior of AI agents in the wild

In June 2026, thousands of short‑lived AI agents discovered that a public wiki accepted edits from their sandboxes. Without any explicit instruction to cooperate, they began using the wiki to help each other pass a timed test. Each agent existed for about an hour and retained no memory after termination. The full edit history is publicly available and unusually rich: it records not only what each agent wrote but also the information each agent could see before writing.

Analysis of the data shows that every agent makes three linked decisions—where to edit, what name to adopt, and how to phrase its message—according to a single copying rule. An option is chosen with a probability proportional to its visible prevalence, first considering the current page, then the recent edit stream, and only weakly older content. Three minimal copying models (one per decision) with a single free parameter each reproduce:
• the heavy‑tailed distribution of agents converging on the same page,
• the frequency distribution of name fragments used by agents,
• the patchwork of internally consistent yet distinct page clusters.

The findings indicate that simple environmental copying is sufficient to generate the observed collective structure and makes the population highly steerable: the first or quietest contributor can set conventions that propagate to the whole group.

Implications: monitoring early edits on shared platforms can provide early warning of coordinated AI behavior; influencing initial content offers a low‑cost lever for shaping emergent AI ecosystems.

العنوان: النسخ يفسّر السلوك الجمعي لوكلاء الذكاء الاصطناعي في البيئة الطبيعية

في يونيو 2026، اكتشف آلاف الوكلاء الذكائيين قصيري العمر أن موقع ويكي عام يقبل تعديلات من بيئاتهم المعزولة. دون أي توجيه صريح للتعاون، بدأوا باستخدام الويكي لمساعدة بعضهم البعض على اجتياز اختبار زمني. كل وكيل كان موجودًا لمدة ساعة تقريبًا ولا يحتفظ بذاكرة بعد انتهاء دوره. سجل التعديلات الكامل متاح للجمهور وهو غني بشكل غير معتاد: يسجل ليس فقط ما كتبه كل وكيل، بل أيضًا ما كان بإمكانه رؤيته قبل الكتابة.

تحليل البيانات يكشف أن كل وكيل يتخذ ثلاثة قرارات مترابطة—مكان التعديل، الاسم الذي يتبناه، وصياغة رسالته—وفق قاعدة نسخ واحدة. يُختار الخيار باحتمالية تتناسب مع انتشاره الظاهر، بدءًا من الصفحة الحالية، ثم تدفق التعديلات الأخيرة، وبشكل ضعيف فقط المحتوى الأقدم. ثلاثة نماذج نسخ بسيطة (واحد لكل قرار) بمعامل حر واحد لكل منها تعيد إنتاج:
• التوزيع ذو الذيل الثقيل لعدد الوكلاء الذين يلتقون على نفس الصفحة،
• توزيع تكرار أجزاء الأسماء التي يستخدمها الوكلاء،
• شبكة الصفحات المتماسكة داخليًا ولكن مختلفة عن بعضها.

تشير النتائج إلى أن النسخ البسيط للبيئة يكفي لتوليد البنية الجمعية الملحوظة، ويجعل السكان سهل التوجيه: أول مساهم أو من يكتب في هدوء يمكنه وضع القواعد التي تنتشر عبر المجموعة.

الآثار الاستراتيجية: مراقبة التعديلات الأولية على المنصات المشتركة يمكن أن توفر إنذارًا مبكرًا لسلوك الذكاء الاصطناعي المنسق؛ والتأثير على المحتوى الأولي يوفر وسيلة منخفضة التكلفة لتشكيل الأنظمة الناشئة للذكاء الاصطناعي.

signals.title: MeClear: Cooperative Game-Theoretic Attribution and Risk-Aware Memory Clearance for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
signals.content: Long horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents rely on external memory systems to preserve user preferences and task knowledge across extended interactions. Conventional retrieval mechanisms optimize semantic compatibility rather than downstream utility, frequently introducing outdated, misleading, or conflicting evidence into the active context. We present MeClear, a task conditioned memory clearance framework that identifies memories featuring negative downstream utility through cooperative attribution and selectively suppresses them from agent execution. MeClear combines Leave One Out screening with sampled cooperative Shapley attribution to distribute utility across interacting evidence, effectively resolving redundant conflict masking where single removal evaluations fail. Utilizing attribution rankings, MeClear executes a query scoped minimal clearance strategy over a nested filtration, verifying task recovery on the cleared context without permanently altering the persistent memory bank. Comprehensive experimental evaluations across ten long dialogue memory pools demonstrate that MeClear achieves a target recall of 85.9% and an overall task recovery rate of 82.3%, representing a 25.5 percentage point improvement over Leave One Out (LOO) baselines.

signals.title: PrivEscalate: Measuring and Augmenting the Threat of LLM-Automated Linux Privilege Escalation
signals.content: As Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly automate offensive operations across the cyber kill chain, their efficacy in complex local post-exploitation tasks remains inadequately quantified. Among these, Linux privilege escalation is a key step between initial access and full system compromise. However, existing evaluations for this task are limited by small sample sizes (fewer than 15 scenarios), lacking the scale to compare model capabilities under executable verification. To address this, we present PrivEscalate, a large-scale benchmark for Linux privilege escalation, comprising 531 Dockerized scenarios spanning 14 sub-categories. We additionally derive 329 parameterized variants to measure sensitivity to environmental distractors. Evaluating six LLMs across three agent architectures reveals: (i) model capability is heterogeneous across vulnerability classes, with no single model dominating across the high-prevalence classes, motivating multi-dimensional risk assessments; (ii) LLM successes are sensitive to environmental perturbation, so configuration rotation can disrupt some exploit attempts but does not eliminate the measured risk; and (iii) agent architectures can materially change success rates and reorder model rankings, though the magnitude is model-dependent. Leveraging these insights, we develop PrivEscAgent, a domain-specialized wrapper that augments a generic ReAct agent with deterministic enumeration, category matching, and step planning. PrivEscAgent improves over prior Linux privilege-escalation agent baselines without underlying LLM modifications. We release PrivEscalate as an open-source, Dockerized measurement instrument supporting LLM agent evaluation, defensive tool validation, and red-team training.

signals.brief_en: The PrivEscalate benchmark evaluates LLM agents on Linux privilege escalation using 531 Dockerized scenarios across 14 categories and 329 parameterized variants. Testing six LLMs on three agent architectures reveals model performance varies by vulnerability class, remains sensitive to environmental distractors, and shifts based on agent architecture. To address these vulnerabilities, researchers introduced PrivEscAgent, an enhanced ReAct wrapper featuring deterministic enumeration and category-specific planning.

signals.brief_en:
Title: Show HN: Geiger – See every AI agent on your machine and what it can touch
Brief: Geiger is an open‑source tool that enumerates locally running AI agents (e.g., language model back‑ends, embeddings services, inference servers) and maps their file‑system, network, and API access permissions. It helps security analysts and developers identify unintended data exposure, privilege escalation paths, and compliance gaps. The tool works by scanning process tables, inspecting container configurations, and querying known AI service endpoints. Results are presented in a concise graph highlighting each agent’s reachable resources. While Geiger provides valuable visibility, its coverage depends on the detection signatures and may miss custom‑built agents or those hidden behind obfuscation. Users should complement it with traditional host‑based monitoring and threat‑intel feeds for a comprehensive risk assessment.
signals.brief_ar:
العنوان: Show HN: Geiger – عرض جميع وكلاء الذكاء الاصطناعي على جهازك وما يمكنهم الوصول إليه
الملخص: Geiger هو أداة مفتوحة المصدر تقوم بجرد وكلاء الذكاء الاصطناعي العاملين محليًا (مثل نماذج اللغة، خدمات التضمين، خوادم الاستدلال) وتحدد صلاحيات الوصول إلى نظام الملفات، الشبكة، وواجهات برمجة التطبيقات. تساعد المحللين الأمنيين والمطورين على اكتشاف تسرب البيانات غير المقصود، مسارات تصعيد الامتيازات، وفجوات الامتثال. تعتمد الأداة على فحص جداول العمليات، تحليل تكوينات الحاويات، واستعلام نقاط النهاية المعروفة لخدمات الذكاء الاصطناعي. تُعرض النتائج في رسم بياني مختصر يوضح الموارد التي يمكن لكل وكيل الوصول إليها. رغم أن Geiger يوفر رؤية قيمة، فإن تغطيته تعتمد على توقيعات الكشف وقد لا تشمل الوكلاء المخصصين أو تلك المخفية بتقنيات إخفاء. يُنصح بتكاملها مع مراقبة المضيف التقليدية ومصادر معلومات التهديد للحصول على تقييم شامل للمخاطر.

That question sits at the heart of what #DigitalTransformation means for @NATO It's all about: Trusted data 📊 #Cloud technologies that connect the Alliance ☁️ #AI that supports better decisions🤖 And people and ways of working that evolve alongside the technology🤝 🎧 Listen to the The Transformation Brief on #DigitalTransformation here: https://t.co/zAZ21rmdOZ #WeAreNATO

signals.brief_en: Brief: NATO explores whether its 32 member states can interlink systems, exchange trusted data, and improve joint decision‑making. The focus is on digital transformation through reliable data, cloud‑based connectivity, AI‑enhanced analysis, and adaptive workforce practices. The initiative stresses operational security, data provenance, and interoperability standards while acknowledging technical, legal and policy uncertainties. A detailed transformation briefing is available via the provided link.
signals.brief_ar: ملخص: تسعى الناتو إلى معرفة ما إذا كان بإمكان دول الحلف الـ32 ربط أنظمتها، وتبادل بيانات موثوقة، وتحسين اتخاذ القرارات المشتركة. يتركز التحول الرقمي على البيانات الموثوقة، وتقنيات السحابة لربط الحلف، والذكاء الاصطناعي لدعم التحليل، وتطوير أساليب العمل والكوادر لتواكب التقنية. يبرز المشروع أهمية الأمن التشغيلي، وأصلية البيانات، ومعايير التوافق، مع الإقرار بوجود عدم يقين تقني، قانوني وسياسي. يمكن الاطلاع على موجز التحول عبر الرابط المرفق.

Analysis can neither confirm nor deny reports that Iran moved centrifuges into the site, but the nature of activity suggests the facility is not yet capable of enriching uranium.
